title: The Sun Will Swell 200 Times Wider: How It All Ends
alt_titles: How the Solar System Ends, in 7 Real Numbers
Earth Has About 1 Billion Years. The Sun Has More
description_intro: How our Solar System ends, step by step, using ESA Gaia results on the Sun's past and future, NASA pages on stellar evolution and the Sun, and the 2025 Hubble and Gaia study on the Milky Way and Andromeda. Dates far in the future are model estimates, and NASA pages differ on some of them.
tags: what happens when the sun dies

sources.title: ESA: Gaia reveals the past and future of the Sun

beats.say: How long do you think our Sun has left? The honest answer is stranger than any doomsday movie.
ESA's article on Gaia gives our Sun an age of around 4.57 billion years: in its comfortable middle age.
By the end you'll know what Gaia's study of Sun-like stars says happens to our Sun as it ages.
Here is your first guess. What ends first: life on Earth, the planet Mercury, or the Sun itself?
Right now the Sun is stable. It fuses hydrogen into helium in a core of about 15 million degrees Celsius.
It sits about 150 million kilometers away, yet its light still warms every ocean you have ever swum in.
That fusion pushes outward against gravity. As long as the push and the pull stay balanced, the Sun stays the Sun.
It is huge. According to NASA, it would take 1.3 million Earths to fill the Sun's volume.
And it holds 99.8% of all the mass in our Solar System. Everything else, you included, is a rounding error.
But fuel never lasts forever. So what runs out first, and what does that mean for the planet you are sitting on?
Here is the twist most people miss. Earth does not wait for the Sun to die. Our deadline comes much sooner.
NASA's article on the Hubble and Gaia galaxy study states it: the warming Sun makes Earth uninhabitable in roughly 1 billion years.
Today the Sun's surface glows at an effective temperature of 5772 Kelvin. A hotter, brighter Sun pours more heat onto us.
Comparing it with Sun-like stars of different ages, the Gaia team found it reaches a maximum temperature at approximately 8 billion years of age.
Subtract today's age and that peak is about 3.43 billion years away. Earth's deadline comes long before that.
So life on Earth runs out of time first, billions of years before the red giant. Did you guess that? Tell me in the comments.
beats.ask: Did you guess Earth would lose the race first?

beats.say: To find this, Gaia's team picked stars with the same mass and chemistry as the Sun, but different ages.
They found 5863 solar analogues. Lined up by age, those stars trace our Sun's past and its future.
That is the beauty of the method. You cannot watch one star for billions of years, but you can watch thousands at once.
And what those stars show next is far more dramatic than a hot planet. What happens when the core runs dry?
When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats up. The outside does the opposite.
According to NASA, the Sun will become a red giant in about 5 billion years. ESA's Gaia study of Sun-like stars puts it around 10–11 billion years of age.
The outer layers swell to up to about 200 times the current solar radius. Picture standing next to that.
Its diameter today is about 1.4 million kilometers. As a red giant, it would stretch across the orbits of Mercury and Venus.
Today the Sun's radius is 695,700 kilometers. Two hundred times that is about 139 million kilometers.
Now compare. Earth orbits at a mean distance of 149.6 million kilometers from the Sun.
That is uncomfortably close. According to NASA, the red giant will engulf Mercury and Venus, and possibly Earth as well.
Venus, our closest planetary neighbour, would be swallowed by the same star that has kept it warm for billions of years.
Astronomers can already tell apart red giants that have not reached their maximum radius from those that have ignited helium.
So far: a red giant up to about 200 times wider, engulfing Mercury and Venus, and possibly Earth. Is that an explosion?
Here is the myth to drop. Our Sun will never go supernova. It does not have the mass.
NASA explains that neutron stars, the leftovers of supernovae, come from stars with between about eight and 20 times the Sun's mass.
Those heavy stars fuse heavier and heavier elements, until the core collapses, rebounds, and the star blows up as a supernova.
What is left of them can be a neutron star. Some of those, called pulsars, spin faster than blender blades.
A star like ours below eight solar masses takes the quieter road: red giant, then a slow unravelling.
If calm cosmic numbers like these make your day, follow the channel. There is a new one every day.
And if you want to find these objects in your own sky, our beginner's guide LOOK UP shows you where. The link in the description.
Main sequence stars range from a tenth to 200 times the Sun's mass. Ours sits near the bottom of that range.
Main sequence stars make up around 90% of the universe's stars. The Sun is ordinary, and ordinary stars die gently.
But gently does not mean quietly. What does a giant star do once it has swallowed its neighbours?
The red giant does not stay at full size. When its core gets hot enough, helium ignites.
Helium starts fusing into carbon, which also releases energy. For a while, that new fuel props the star up again.
ESA's Gaia team describes what happens next: the star recedes to a radius of about 10 times the current solar value.
Ten times wider than today is still a giant star, just far smaller than its peak of about 200 times.
Then the giant becomes unstable. In NASA's description it starts pulsating, expanding and throwing off parts of its atmosphere.
Eventually all the outer layers blow away into an expanding cloud of dust and gas called a planetary nebula.
You have probably seen one in a photo. That glowing shell is a dying star giving its material back to the galaxy.
Sun-like stars of every age in Gaia's data are how astronomers piece together these late stages of a star like ours.
Gaia's catalogue holds about 440,000 orbital solutions for binary stars: pairs born together, with the same age, to test these stages.
Quick recap: a giant that shrinks to about 10 times today's size, pulses, and blows away its outer layers. So what is left in the middle?
What remains is the bare core: a white dwarf. According to NASA, a white dwarf is usually Earth-size but hundreds of thousands of times more massive.
Think about that squeeze. The Sun's radius today is 695,700 kilometers. Earth's is 6371.
That is a ratio of 109.2. A white dwarf Sun would be squeezed down to about Earth's size.
A teaspoon of white dwarf material would weigh more than a pickup truck. Would you try to lift it?
It makes no new heat. It just glows and slowly cools over billions of years.
Despite the name, white dwarfs can glow from blue white to red as they slowly cool.
When does the Sun reach this stage? NASA pages give about 8 billion years and about 10 billion years from now.

show.title: WHITE DWARF SUN, YEARS FROM NOW

beats.say: And the surviving outer planets? NASA's Spitzer found about 40 white dwarfs with hot, dusty disks.
Astronomers think leftover planets can fling small rocky bodies inward, where the dead star tears them apart.
So the Sun ends as a faint, cooling ember. Or could something even bigger reach us first?
You have probably heard that our galaxy will crash into Andromeda. As far back as 1912, astronomers saw it heading our way.
In 2012, Hubble data made a direct impact look almost certain, in no more than 5 billion years.
Then a new study used Hubble and Gaia together. It tested 22 different variables and ran 100,000 simulations.
The result: approximately a 50-50 chance of the two galaxies colliding within the next 10 billion years.
The chance of a head-on collision in only 4 to 5 billion years is just around 2%.
Andromeda's satellite galaxy M33 pulls us a little toward it, while the Large Magellanic Cloud pulls the Milky Way away.
In about half the simulations the galaxies pass each other at around half a million light-years, then merge in the far future.
So the Sun's own story ends first. As the researchers put it, Andromeda is the least of our cosmic worries.
Earth uninhabitable in roughly 1 billion years, a red giant in about 5 billion, a white dwarf after that. The galaxy? A coin toss.
If you want to see Andromeda yourself, a faint smudge you can find on a dark night, LOOK UP shows you how. Link in the description.
Which ending surprised you most: Earth's deadline, the giant Sun or the coin toss? Write it below.
